generic_name: ferric iron (ferric carboxymaltose / ferric maltol / ferric derisomaltose depending on formulation)
purpose: Ferric iron is used to treat iron deficiency anemia, which means your body does not have enough iron to make healthy red blood cells. Your doctor may prescribe it if you are not getting enough iron from food or other iron pills, or if your body cannot absorb iron well. It helps restore your iron levels so you feel less tired and more energetic.
how_it_works: Iron is a mineral your body needs to make hemoglobin, which is the part of your red blood cells that carries oxygen throughout your body. When you take ferric iron, your body converts it into a form it can use and stores it to build new, healthy red blood cells. Think of it like refilling your body's iron tank so your blood can carry oxygen properly again.
common_side_effects: Common side effects include nausea, stomach upset, constipation, diarrhea, dark or tarry stools (this is normal with iron), and headache. If given as an injection, you might notice some flushing, dizziness, or temporary changes in blood pressure. Dark stools are expected and not a reason to worry.
warnings: Tell your doctor if you have had allergic reactions to iron products before, since serious allergic reactions are possible especially with the injectable form. Do not take iron supplements if you have too much iron in your body (a condition called hemochromatosis). Keep iron supplements out of reach of children, as accidental overdose in young children can be very dangerous. Let your doctor know all medications you take, since iron can affect how some other medicines are absorbed.
typical_dosing: Dosing depends on which form you are taking. The capsule form (Accrufer) is usually taken twice a day with food. The injectable forms (Injectafer, Monofer) are given by a nurse or doctor through an IV, often as one or two doses based on your weight and iron levels. Always follow your doctor or pharmacist's exact instructions for your specific product.
